1.1.b:
A replaced hip is a few parts that carry load and rub; first, what goes where.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which material goes where?"
- "The **stem** is always metal, because it is loaded millions of times."
- "The **head** is always hard: cobalt-chrome or ceramic."
- "The commonest bearing now is metal or ceramic on **HXLPE** (highly cross-linked polyethylene)."

### Components and Their Materials
Each part has one job, and the job picks the material.

#### Stem and Acetabular Shell
- The **stem** is always metal, and it gives primary fixation
- It is loaded millions of times, so it needs high **fatigue strength**
- Stems are α+β or β **titanium alloys**; cups are **titanium** shells

#### Femoral Head and Liner
- The **head** must be hard, because its whole surface is always loaded
- Each point of the liner is loaded only part of the time
- So the liner may be hard or soft; a soft partner always sits there

MEMORY HOOK — full time, part time
- The head works full time, the liner part time: the hard material gets the full-time job.

### The Bearing Surface
The bearing is where the head meets the liner.
- The **friction interface** is the head–liner contact
[[FIG: Fig 1.1 · 1.1
- Metal on **UHMWPE** (ultra-high-molecular-weight PE) was the historical standard
- Today HXLPE on a cobalt-chrome or ceramic head is the dominant couple (Campbell)
- A bigger head in the same cup thins the PE (polyethylene): avoid conventional PE **<6 mm**
- Hard-on-hard may be mixed: a ceramic head on a metal liner joins the merits of both

### Mechanical Properties of Materials
A **biomaterial** is any substance used to treat, augment or replace a tissue or function.

#### Definitions
Learn the vocabulary once; Prof Fahmy builds it on the stress–strain curve.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Brittle** vs **ductile** | little plastic deformation (glass, ceramic) vs much (stainless steel) |
| **Notch sensitivity** | fracture from a crack or scratch; high in brittle materials |
| **Hardness** | resists scratching and indentation; highest in **ceramic** |

#### Stiffness and Toughness
- The **elastic zone** is reversible; the **plastic zone** leaves a permanent change of shape
- **Young's modulus** is the elastic slope of the stress–strain curve
- Its order: ceramic > metal alloys > cortical bone > cement > PE
[[FIG: Fig 1.2 · 1.1
- **Toughness** is the area under the curve: the energy absorbed
- It beats ultimate tensile strength: at the same peak, the larger area is the ductile material
[[FIG: Fig 1.3 · 1.1

#### Joint Reaction Force
- The hip carries **3×** body weight walking, ≈**5×** on stairs or jogging
[[FIG: Fig 1.4 · 1.1
- So an 80-kg patient walking uphill puts ≈400 kg across the hip (Prof Fawzy)

1.2.b:
Metals carry the load; their price is corrosion and stress shielding.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which metal, and what is stress shielding?"
- "Heads are **cobalt-chrome**; uncemented stems and cups are **titanium**."
- "Titanium stays off bearings because it **scratches and wears**."
- "A stiff stem takes the load, so the proximal femur thins: **stress shielding**."

### Orthopaedic Metals
An **alloy** is a metal plus other elements, so it is stronger, harder and resists corrosion.

#### Properties of the Four Metals

| Metal (Prof Fahmy) | Strength | Weakness | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stainless steel** | very stiff | stress shielding, corrosion | cemented stems |
| **Cobalt-chromium** | corrosion resistant, low wear, highest modulus | stress shielding | **heads**, cemented stems |
| **Titanium** | biocompatible, low modulus | poor wear | uncemented stems, cups |
| **Tantalum** | low modulus, very porous | expensive | acetabular reconstruction, cup revision |

- A stiff stainless steel stem bends less, so the cement mantle is protected
[[FIG: Fig 1.5 · 1.2

#### Cobalt-Chromium Femoral Heads
- The head is **cobalt-chrome**: stiff, least toxic and bioinert; stainless steel is not
[[FIG: Fig 1.6 · 1.2
- Titanium stays off bearings because it **scratches and wears**, not because it is "too flexible" (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 1.7 · 1.2

#### Titanium and Bone Ingrowth
- Titanium does not irritate tissue, and its modulus sits just above cortical bone
- Titanium gives denser bone and more ingrowth than cobalt-chrome

### Corrosion
Metals have one way of failing that the other materials lack.

#### Modes of Material Failure
- All materials fail by **wear** and **fatigue**; metals also fail by **corrosion**
[[FIG: Fig 1.8 · 1.2
- **Fatigue failure** comes below the ultimate tensile stress, from repeated loading
- **Wear** is a mechanical loss of material; corrosion is a chemical loss

#### Types of Corrosion

| Corrosion | Where it happens |
|---|---|
| **Galvanic** | two different metals form cathode and anode, e.g. stainless steel + cobalt-chrome, so never mix them |
| **Crevice** | in cracks or scratches; stainless steel is most prone, so do not scratch it at insertion |
| **Fretting** | micromotion; always at the head–neck junction |

#### Trunnionosis
- **Trunnionosis** is fretting corrosion between the stem trunnion and a cobalt-chrome head
- It leads to **ALTR** (adverse local tissue reaction), and it is commoner than once thought
- So ceramic and ceramicised metal heads are used more widely (Campbell)

### Stress Shielding
Stiffness matters again here, because bone grows where it is loaded.

#### Mechanism
- A stiff stem takes the load, so the proximal femur is unloaded
[[FIG: Fig 1.9 · 1.2
- Unloaded bone resorbs: **Wolff's law** in reverse
- The mismatch puts high stress at the **distal tip**; elsewhere bone atrophies from disuse

#### Radiographic and Clinical Features
- A stiff cobalt-chrome stem gives thigh pain; a fully porous stem loads the diaphysis
- It occurs with **23%** of fully porous stems and **18%** of AML (anatomic medullary locking) stems

MEMORY HOOK — the overprotective parent
- A stiff stem is an overprotective parent: it carries every load, so the proximal femur thins.

#### Risk Factors
| Factor | Higher risk |
|---|---|
| Material | cobalt-chrome > titanium |
| Coating | extensive > proximal · rigid fixation |
| Design | solid > hollow |
| Diameter | larger: +20% ≈ 2× stiffness (radius⁴) |
| Bone | preoperative osteopenia |

#### Prevention
- **Proximal-only porous coating** shields less and keeps fixation intact
[[FIG: Fig 1.10 · 1.2
- A **tapered titanium stem** osseointegrates by ≈12 weeks: graded load, less thigh pain

#### Clinical Significance
- At 14 years, bone loss came without more revision, osteolysis or thigh pain
- It matters at **revision**: too little bone is left for a standard proximal-fit stem

PITFALL — calcar rounding on a fixed stem
- **Calcar rounding** and **Gruen zone 1 and 7** thinning around a fixed stem are not loosening.
- Say → "This is stress shielding around a well-fixed stem, not loosening."

- The Gruen zones themselves → 06 Post-op radiograph

1.3.b:
Ceramic is the hardest bearing: low wear, but a risk of fracture.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "tell me about ceramic bearings"
- "Ceramic is **hard and brittle**: strong in compression, weak in bending."
- "Today's ceramic is **AMC** (alumina matrix composite, BIOLOX delta): minimal wear, very low fracture risk."
- "After a fracture, revise to ceramic: **once a ceramic, always a ceramic**."

### Bearing Ceramics
Ceramics are inorganic compounds held by ionic and covalent bonds; the two bearing ceramics are **alumina** and **zirconia**.

#### Alumina and Zirconia
- **CoC** (ceramic-on-ceramic) means alumina-on-alumina, because zirconia wears badly against itself
- Ceramic is strong in compression but weak in bending: **hard and brittle**
[[FIG: Fig 1.11 · 1.3

#### Material Properties
- It is the stiffest material and does not deform, so it never makes a stem
- So ceramic is used for the head and liner only; alumina is the most inert
- Its particles are **bioinert**: no allergic or inflammatory reaction, no ions, no systemic effect
- Ceramic is **hydrophilic**: wettable, so friction is low

| Ceramic (Prof Fahmy) | Wear | Fracture risk |
|---|---|---|
| Alumina | very low | brittle |
| Zirconia | higher | lower |
| **AMC** (BIOLOX delta) | minimal | very low |

#### Alumina Matrix Composite
- **AMC** joins alumina's surface to zirconia's strength: ≈50–60% tougher than alumina
- Generations ran from 1974 to **BIOLOX delta** in 2003: smaller grains, far fewer fractures
[[FIG: Fig 1.12 · 1.3
- **Oxidized zirconium** is a metal alloy with a ceramic surface, not a solid ceramic
- It has no nickel, so it suits metal hypersensitivity; it runs only against PE
- It is damaged more than ceramic after a dislocation

#### Withdrawal of Pure Zirconia
- In body fluid zirconia changes phase: weaker, rougher, more wear
- **Yttria-stabilised** zirconia turns tetragonal to monoclinic, and its grains expand 4%
- A recall after ball fractures ended it in 2001; m-ZR is still used
- Zirconia stays in dental prostheses but not in joint bearings

### Ceramic Fracture
Brittleness is the price of hardness: micro-cracks spread, and trauma completes the break.

#### Incidence
- Early ceramics fractured often; the Morse taper (1977) brought it to 2%, and now **0.004%**
- Delta ceramic breaks in ≈1 in 100,000 (0.001%); pure alumina in 1 in 5000 (0.02%)

#### Risk Reduction
- Fracture is commoner with small heads and **short necks**: less ceramic around the taper bore
- A 32-mm head is 60% stronger than a 28-mm head
- Keep cup abduction **<50°**; fracture rises with poor technique, e.g. cup **retroversion**

#### Revision After Fracture
Prof Fawzy gives the steps.
- **BIOLOX delta** is pink, and its fracture is often unseen on X-ray
[[FIG: Fig 1.13 · 1.3
- A ball broken in half on the film is ceramic: metal never breaks in half
[[FIG: Fig 1.14 · 1.3
- So pain or a squeak calls for **CT**, possibly fluid analysis, then revision as soon as possible
- Revise to a **ceramic head**: leftover ceramic is a third body that destroys a metal head
- A ceramic liner needs a suction instrument to come out; pulling the head damages the taper

#### Management of the Taper
- Taper intact and stem stable: a ceramic head with a **metal sleeve**
- Taper damaged: revise the stem
[[FIG: Fig 1.15 · 1.3

MEMORY HOOK — grit in the gearbox
- Ceramic crumbs are grit in a gearbox: they grind a metal head away. Once a ceramic, always a ceramic.

### Advantages and Disadvantages
Ceramic wins on wear and loses on forgiveness.

#### Advantages
- **Less wear and osteolysis**, so it is still advised for young adults
- Alumina-on-alumina liner wear is 4000× less than cobalt-chrome on PE (Campbell)
- Measured wear stayed <0.025 mm/year at 18.5 years
- It resists scratches, so third-body wear is less
[[FIG: Fig 1.16 · 1.3
- A scratch on ceramic is a V-shaped pit; on metal it raises asperities that wear PE
- Water spreads on ceramic: contact angle 45° vs 86° on metal (Prof Fawzy)
[[FIG: Fig 1.17 · 1.3
- Large databases report fewer infections with ceramic bearings

#### Squeaking
- **Squeaking** is specific to CoC: edge loading after malposition, with rim impingement and stripe wear
- Other causes: poor lubrication, and a flexible stem amplifies the vibration
- It is usually low, but >10% in some series, and 23% with 32–48 mm delta heads (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 1.18 · 1.3
- Prof Fahmy quotes up to 30%; it starts after >1 year, often on stairs

#### Practical Limitations
- Fracture is not eliminated; there are no lipped inserts and modularity is limited
[[FIG: Fig 1.19 · 1.3
- Offset liners and skirted heads are absent, and neck lengths are few
- The insert may chip at impaction; neck–rim impingement notches the metal neck
- A vertical cup raises ceramic wear
- It needs exact positioning, and it is expensive: not forgiving, with a learning curve

1.4.b:
PE is the weakest link, so how it is made decides how long it lasts.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how is polyethylene made wear-resistant?"
- "Gamma **in air** oxidises PE; gamma **without oxygen** cross-links it."
- "Cross-linking (HXLPE) cuts wear by **40–95%**, but costs fatigue strength."
- "Leftover radicals are removed by remelting or held by **vitamin E**."

### Structure and Manufacture
Wear starts in the factory, long before the theatre.

#### Molecule
- **UHMWPE** is a linear homopolymer of >200,000 monomers
- Cross-links tie the chains, resisting intermolecular mobility, so deformation and wear fall
[[FIG: Fig 1.20 · 1.4

#### Moulding
- Ethylene (C2H4) is polymerised into powder, then consolidated and shaped
[[FIG: Fig 1.21 · 1.4
- **Direct compression moulding** gives half the clinical wear of machined PE
- **Ram-bar extrusion** adds calcium stearate to ease flow; the impurity raises wear

### Sterilisation and Free Radicals
Irradiation breaks a covalent bond and leaves a **free radical**.

#### Effect of Oxygen
- With oxygen, the radical degrades the PE; without oxygen, it forms a cross-link
[[FIG: Fig 1.22 · 1.4

| Sterilisation (Prof Fahmy) | Effect |
|---|---|
| Ethylene oxide, gas plasma | no cross-linking, properties unchanged, so inferior wear |
| Gamma in air (cobalt-60, 2–4 Mrad) | radicals + oxygen: **oxidation**, so weak PE |
| Gamma in vacuum or inert gas | radicals form **cross-links**, so wear falls |

#### Retrieval Findings
- Irradiation **creates** radicals and never removes them; heat or vitamin E does
- Gamma-in-air PE shows a subsurface **white band** of oxidation on retrieval

MEMORY HOOK — the open milk bottle
- Gamma in air is a milk bottle left open: radicals meet oxygen and the PE goes off.

### Highly Cross-Linked Polyethylene
More cross-links mean less wear, but a stiffer, weaker plastic.

#### Benefits
- **HXLPE** cuts wear by 40–95%, with smaller particles (Surgery of the Hip)
[[FIG: Fig 1.23 · 1.4
- Prof Fahmy gives 55–90%; hip simulators show 80–90% (Campbell)
- A larger head on HXLPE gives no rise in volumetric wear
- Its wear did not change with head size from 22 to 46 mm
- So 32, 36 and 40 mm heads go on HXLPE only; UHMWPE brings late osteolysis (Prof Fady Kamal)
[[FIG: Fig 1.24 · 1.4
- An HXLPE liner can be exchanged without revising a well-fixed shell

#### Drawbacks
- Doses up to **8–10 Mrad** add wear resistance but lower fatigue and fracture strength
- Campbell gives 5–10 Mrad for cross-linking
- Thin or unsupported HXLPE at the rim lock may suffer **rim fracture**
[[FIG: Fig 1.25 · 1.4

### Thermal Treatment
Heat clears the radicals, but each way of heating has its own weakness.

| Heat (Prof Fahmy) | Radicals | Crystallinity | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Remelting** (above ≈135 °C) | all removed | falls (40%) | fatigue cracking |
| **Annealing** (below melting) | remain | kept (60%) | in-vivo oxidation |

- The crystalline phase gives the strength
- Other answers: **vitamin E**, which holds radicals without remelting's strength loss, or sequential irradiation + annealing
- HXLPE is then sterilised by gas plasma or ethylene oxide, because gamma would add radicals

### Shelf Life and Oxidation
Oxygen keeps working after the packet is sealed.

#### Oxidation
- Oxygen re-enters on the shelf and in vivo
- On the shelf, radicals meet oxygen, so the PE oxidises and wears
- The change becomes visible after >4 years
[[FIG: Fig 1.26 · 1.4
- It was found after Charnley's era, in cups cut after long storage

#### Clinical Significance
- Oxidation cuts toughness and fatigue strength, so failure can be catastrophic
- It is irreversible, so prevent it

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Air oxidises · no air cross-links · melt or vitamin E mops up · old stock goes off after 4 years**

Heat clears the radicals, but each way of heating has its own weakness.

|---|---|---|---|

- It was found after Charnley's era, in cups cut after long storage

#### Clinical Significance
- Oxidation cuts toughness and fatigue strength, so failure can be catastrophic
- It is irreversible, so prevent it

- **Ceramic-on-PE** avoids brittleness and releases fewer ions than MoM

| Modularity | common, cheap couples high; rare, dear ones low |

1.6.b:
MoM wore 40–100× less than metal-on-PE, so why did most of it go?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why was MoM withdrawn?"
- "Metal ions and **ALVAL** led to pseudotumour, so most MoM was withdrawn."
- "A painful MoM hip needs serum **cobalt and chromium** and **MARS-MRI**."
- "No MoM in **renal impairment** or in women who may conceive."

### Contraindications
The ions are the problem, and they travel.

#### Systemic Distribution of Ions
- MoM toxicity: renal failure, crossing the placenta, early pseudotumour, nickel urticaria
- The ions are cleared by the kidney
- So no MoM in **renal impairment** or in women who may conceive, because ions are teratogenic

### Adverse Reactions to Metal Debris
The trouble came from the ions and the tissue reaction.

#### Metal Ions
- Concerns were lymphocytic aggregates, **metal ions** and hypersensitivity
[[FIG: Fig 1.31 · 1.6
- Large-head modular MoM raised cobalt and chromium sharply, and the junctions were blamed

#### Ion Kinetics
- **Run-in**: ions rise in the first year, then fall (Prof Fawzy)
- A later rise means trouble

#### Tissue Reaction
- **ALVAL** (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion) leads to pseudotumour
[[FIG: Fig 1.32 · 1.6
- So most MoM implants were withdrawn
- The reaction is **ALTR / ARMD** (adverse local tissue reaction / reaction to metal debris)

#### Local and Systemic Effects
- Debris triggers a dose-related allergic response, local or systemic
[[FIG: Fig 1.33 · 1.6
- Local effects are metallosis, pseudotumour and bone loss
- Systemic effects are raised ions and toxicity; carcinogenesis is only weak speculation
- A painful MoM hip needs serum **cobalt and chromium** and **MARS-MRI** (metal artefact reduction sequence)
- Aspiration completes the work-up

### Hip Resurfacing
Resurfacing is the other MoM use, with its own rules.

#### Advantages and Risks
- Resurfacing preserves femoral bone stock
- MoM **resurfacing** risks neck fracture and notching, and it is technique-sensitive
[[FIG: Fig 1.34 · 1.6
- Fracture follows a small neck, not stem size

#### Patient Selection
- It is not for females, because their necks are small, not only for pregnancy
- Indications: **males**, a large head, the McMinn (Birmingham) hip, expertise
- Exclude head cysts, osteonecrosis, renal disease and marked dysplasia; leg-length difference is relative (Campbell)

#### Templating and Follow-Up
- The femoral component should be 2–4 mm wider than the neck
- Equal head and neck widths risk notching the neck
- Review every 12–24 months; ions or metal-subtraction MRI if symptoms appear

PITFALL — resurfacing head size: 48 or 56–64 mm?
- Campbell: men <65, head **≥48 mm**; Prof Fawzy: head **56–64 mm**.
- Say → "Large heads only: at least 48 mm, best results 56–64 mm."

1.7.b:
All this matters because of wear; first, how surfaces lose material.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is wear?"
- "**Wear** is material lost from one surface by another surface."
- "Types say **how**: adhesive, abrasive, third-body, fatigue; modes say **which surfaces** rub."
- "A fluid film needs a large head and a small clearance."

### Definition of Wear
Wear takes three forms in the hip.
- They are **adhesive, abrasive** and **corrosive**
[[FIG: Fig 1.35 · 1.7
- The hip slides in many directions, so crossing tracks make more debris
- The **tribosystem** is two bodies, a lubricant, the environment and a load; its output is particles

### Wear Mechanisms
Each type is a different way of tearing material off.

#### Types of Wear

| Type | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Adhesive** | bonds weld the surfaces; spot welding at the trunnion gives **trunnionosis** |
| **Abrasive** (two-body) | **ploughing**: asperities of the harder surface scratch the PE |
| **Three-body** | debris, cement or bone wedged between the surfaces |
| **Fatigue** | repeated stress; microcracks join and a piece breaks off |
| **Backside** | the liner moves on its metal shell or tibial baseplate |
| **Stripe** | ceramic **edge loading** after microseparation: a stripe on head and liner |

#### Third-Body Wear
- Abrasion is the third-body mechanism: cement particles, worn MoM **carbides**
[[FIG: Fig 1.36 · 1.7
- Third bodies are implant debris, cement, earlier wear debris or bone
- Cement or bone left at closure becomes a third body, so irrigate before reduction

### McKellop Wear Modes
McKellop's modes ask a different question: which surfaces are rubbing?

| McKellop mode (Surgery of the Hip) | What rubs |
|---|---|
| 1 · Regular sliding | the intended bearing surfaces |
| 2 · Impingement | bearing on non-bearing surface, e.g. head on cup edge |
| 3 · Three-body | a third body between the bearing surfaces |
| 4 · Backside (fretting) | two non-bearing surfaces, e.g. backside, taper |

### Specific Wear Patterns
Three patterns are worth knowing by name.

#### Stripe Wear
- **Ceramic** surface pits rub the bearing and wear it
- Stripe causes: negative clearance, vertical or loose cup, microseparation, impingement
[[FIG: Fig 1.37 · 1.7
- Retrievals show edge loading with the hip flexed: rising from a chair, a high step
[[FIG: Fig 1.38 · 1.7

#### Metal Transfer
- **Metal smearing** is cup metal transferred to a ceramic head during subluxation (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 1.39 · 1.7

#### Backside Wear
- It comes from poor locking and a rough shell interior, as in first-generation cementless cups
- **Screw holes** leave the PE unsupported, so it cold-flows
[[FIG: Fig 1.40 · 1.7
- They are also a debris route, so osteolysis appears behind the acetabulum

### Friction and Lubrication
How surfaces rub depends on friction and lubrication.

#### Friction
- **Tribology** is the study of friction, lubrication and wear
- **F = μ × W**: there is no area term (Prof Abo El Soud)
[[FIG: Fig 1.41 · 1.7
- The real contact area is much smaller than the apparent one
- Even polished surfaces are rough: PE ≈1 µm, polished metal ≈0.05 µm

#### Lubrication Regimes
- **Lambda (λ)** is the film thickness divided by the roughness
[[FIG: Fig 1.42 · 1.7
- As λ rises, lubrication passes from boundary to mixed to fluid film
[[FIG: Fig 1.43 · 1.7
- In boundary lubrication single lubricant molecules cling to both surfaces, and asperities still touch
- Above λ 3, friction rises again from viscous drag

#### Fluid-Film Lubrication
- **Hydrostatic** film is pumped (factories); **hydrodynamic** film is made by motion (the body)
- Prof Abo El Soud's water-skier glides with speed, a light load, a small angle and a smooth ski
[[FIG: Fig 1.44 · 1.7
- **Radial clearance** is the liner radius minus the head radius
[[FIG: Fig 1.45 · 1.7
- Too loose gives point loading; too tight seizes at the equator; small clearance with polar contact is ideal
[[FIG: Fig 1.46 · 1.7
- A small clearance draws fluid in: **entrainment**
- At rest only the pole touches; motion starts in boundary lubrication, then builds the film

#### Head Size and Lubrication
- A large head (36 vs 28 mm) slides faster, so it builds a fluid film
- A 28-mm head stays in boundary lubrication, relying on **lubricin**
- Like an engine, the hip needs both the oil film and the boundary additive
- **Charnley** built a low frictional torque arthroplasty: metal-on-PE, with very low friction
[[FIG: Fig 1.47 · 1.7

MEMORY HOOK — aquaplaning
- A fluid film is aquaplaning on purpose: above λ 3 the surfaces never touch.

1.8.t: Wear Measurement and Determinants of Polyethylene Wear
1.8.b:
Next, how wear is measured and what makes PE wear faster.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you measure and reduce PE wear?"
- "**Linear** wear is depth; **volumetric** wear is volume, and volume makes the particles."
- "Osteolysis is uncommon below linear wear of about **0.1 mm a year**."
- "Reduce it: smooth hard head, **HXLPE ≥6 mm**, good cup angle, no third bodies."

### Linear and Volumetric Wear
Two numbers describe wear, and they can point in opposite directions.

#### Definitions and Measurement
- **Linear** wear is the 1-D depth of penetration
[[FIG: Fig 1.48 · 1.8
- **Volumetric** wear is the 3-D volume lost, worked out by software
- On X-ray, use the **Martell** method

#### Radiographic Appearance
- On the AP film the head sits eccentric; the gap narrows superolaterally
- An eccentric head is PE wear, not shortening
[[FIG: Fig 1.49 · 1.8
- Osteolysis around an uncemented cup is particle disease, not a cement problem (Prof Fawzy)

#### Effect of Head Size
- Pressure is load divided by area
- So a small head wears faster in depth, and a large head loses more volume
- A large head's linear wear looks better, but **volumetric** wear drives osteolysis

MEMORY HOOK — two footprints
- A small head leaves a deep, narrow footprint; a big head a shallow, wide one holding more volume.

#### Time Course
- Hard-on-hard bearings **bed in** over ≈1 million cycles (year 1), then wear less
[[FIG: Fig 1.50 · 1.8
- Running-in wear is high, then steady, like a new car's engine
- Any wear curve rises again at the end of life, ending in catastrophic failure

PITFALL — osteolysis threshold: 0.1 or 0.3 mm/year?
- Miller gives linear wear **>0.1 mm/year**; Surgery of the Hip gives 0.3 mm/year.
- Say → "About 0.1 mm a year; below it osteolysis is uncommon (Miller)."

### Determinants of Polyethylene Wear
PE is the most wear-prone part: the **weakest link**.
- Debris is mostly PE; cobalt, titanium and cement add to it (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 1.51 · 1.8

#### Liner Thickness
- A thin liner behaves like the stiff shell, so **contact stress** rises and fatigue comes early
[[FIG: Fig 1.52 · 1.8
- Below **6 mm**, stress and osteolysis rise; below 5 mm, wear and fracture (Surgery of the Hip)
- Yet thin HXLPE liners of 3.9–5.9 mm showed no failure at ≥10 years (Campbell)
- A 1-mm loss is 10% of a 10-mm liner but 20% of a 5-mm one

#### Femoral Head Surface
- Invisible **asperities** on a head scratch the PE
- A head nicked at reduction is the commonest avoidable fault: sandpaper for life
- Trial reductions against retractors or cup edges scratch it, so protect it
- The head must be smooth and spherical; once PE is scratched, it wears faster

#### Head Size
- Wear follows **sliding distance**, so a bigger head wears more volume in conventional PE

#### Cup Position and Patient Activity
- Cup inclination **>50°**, malalignment and unrestored offset increase wear
- **Active** patients make more debris, not heavy ones
- Aerobic exercise is fine; avoid running and heavy lifting

#### In the Knee
- Malalignment concentrates stress, so the insert wears fast and loosens early (Prof Abdel Karim)
- An overcut posterior condyle loses offset: PE–femur impingement and faster wear
- Condylar lift-off loads one side, so PE wear accelerates
- A mobile bearing was meant to lower wear, but backside wear rose; a well-placed fixed bearing lasts as long
- Knee design and bearings → 07 Knee design

What the particles do to bone → 14 Aseptic loosening.

1.8.1.b:
Two numbers describe wear, and they can point in opposite directions.

#### Definitions and Measurement
- **Linear** wear is the 1-D depth of penetration
[[FIG: Fig 1.48 · 1.8
- **Volumetric** wear is the 3-D volume lost, worked out by software
- On X-ray, use the **Martell** method

#### Radiographic Appearance
- On the AP film the head sits eccentric; the gap narrows superolaterally
- An eccentric head is PE wear, not shortening
[[FIG: Fig 1.49 · 1.8
- Osteolysis around an uncemented cup is particle disease, not a cement problem (Prof Fawzy)

#### Effect of Head Size
- Pressure is load divided by area
- So a small head wears faster in depth, and a large head loses more volume
- A large head's linear wear looks better, but **volumetric** wear drives osteolysis

MEMORY HOOK — two footprints
- A small head leaves a deep, narrow footprint; a big head a shallow, wide one holding more volume.

#### Time Course
- Hard-on-hard bearings **bed in** over ≈1 million cycles (year 1), then wear less
[[FIG: Fig 1.50 · 1.8
- Running-in wear is high, then steady, like a new car's engine
- Any wear curve rises again at the end of life, ending in catastrophic failure

PITFALL — osteolysis threshold: 0.1 or 0.3 mm/year?
- Miller gives linear wear **>0.1 mm/year**; Surgery of the Hip gives 0.3 mm/year.
- Say → "About 0.1 mm a year; below it osteolysis is uncommon (Miller)."

1.8.2.b:
PE is the most wear-prone part: the **weakest link**.
- Debris is mostly PE; cobalt, titanium and cement add to it (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 1.51 · 1.8

#### Liner Thickness
- A thin liner behaves like the stiff shell, so **contact stress** rises and fatigue comes early
[[FIG: Fig 1.52 · 1.8
- Below **6 mm**, stress and osteolysis rise; below 5 mm, wear and fracture (Surgery of the Hip)
- Yet thin HXLPE liners of 3.9–5.9 mm showed no failure at ≥10 years (Campbell)
- A 1-mm loss is 10% of a 10-mm liner but 20% of a 5-mm one

#### Femoral Head Surface
- Invisible **asperities** on a head scratch the PE
- A head nicked at reduction is the commonest avoidable fault: sandpaper for life
- Trial reductions against retractors or cup edges scratch it, so protect it
- The head must be smooth and spherical; once PE is scratched, it wears faster

#### Head Size
- Wear follows **sliding distance**, so a bigger head wears more volume in conventional PE

#### Cup Position and Patient Activity
- Cup inclination **>50°**, malalignment and unrestored offset increase wear
- **Active** patients make more debris, not heavy ones
- Aerobic exercise is fine; avoid running and heavy lifting

#### In the Knee
- Malalignment concentrates stress, so the insert wears fast and loosens early (Prof Abdel Karim)
- An overcut posterior condyle loses offset: PE–femur impingement and faster wear
- Condylar lift-off loads one side, so PE wear accelerates
- A mobile bearing was meant to lower wear, but backside wear rose; a well-placed fixed bearing lasts as long
- Knee design and bearings → 07 Knee design

What the particles do to bone → 14 Aseptic loosening.
